title: Scored rounds: were the scores followed?
question: In rounds that publish scores or applicant counts, how many applicants were funded, was anyone funded ahead of a higher-scored rival, and how close were the calls?
finding: Scooter permits, 2019: 4 of 11 applicants were permitted, the 4 highest scores, with no lower score preferred over a higher one. State bond and tax-credit rounds with an award list, 2021 to 2026: San Francisco projects made 64 applications and 33 were funded: 1 of 21 in the first 4 rounds (applications of February 2021 to March 2022), when 45% of all applications statewide were funded, and 32 of 43 since, against 54% statewide. In 2 cases a San Francisco application lost while a lower-scored San Francisco one in the same pool won. Every San Francisco applicant was funded in 9 rounds. Community Challenge Grants, 2023: 24 of 28 applications were funded, in a round whose scoring the Controller later found unreliable.
how: Scooter permits: applicants, total scores and permits as the transportation agency published them. Community Challenge Grants: the counts printed in the Controller’s review. State rounds: every application in the State’s applicant spreadsheet for the round, matched by application number to the round’s award list. "Passed over" counts San Francisco applications that were not funded although they held more points, or the same points and a higher tie-breaker, than a funded San Francisco application in the same pool of the same round. "Closest call" is the smallest tie-breaker gap between a funded and an unfunded San Francisco application with the same points in the same pool. Competitive 9% rounds are matched to the recommendation lists on disk.
limits: The State’s regulations are not on disk. Its lists carry columns for set-asides, geographic regions and State credits, which suggests awards inside a pool do not go on score alone, and statewide such cases are common in the same files, so a "passed over" row is a question for the staff report, not a finding. An application may also have been withdrawn or found ineligible. Scores are self-scores or final scores as the State printed them. Rounds without an award list on disk show applicants only. A round in which every applicant is funded can simply mean money was not short. The swing in San Francisco’s results is set beside the statewide rate only as a yardstick: these are scored rounds, and had awards been drawn by lot at the statewide rate, 1 or fewer wins in 21 would come up about 1 in 16,000 and 32 or more in 43 about 1 in 210; a change in the scoring rules between those years would explain it, and the rules are not on disk.

columns.t: Passed over despite a higher score
